title: Drift: when reality changes behind Terraform
summary: What drift is, how a plan finds it, plan -refresh-only, and the three ways to answer it: put it back, put it in the code, or let another owner have the attribute.

steps.title: Drift
body: **Drift** is any difference between the real objects and what the state says, made outside Terraform: a hotfix in the
console at 3 a.m., a script, another tool, an autoscaler, a colleague who "just quickly" opened a port.
Every plan starts by **refreshing**: it asks the provider for the current value of each object in the state. Then it
plans to make reality match the **code** again. That means a normal `apply` quietly **undoes** the hotfix. To see
only what changed outside, without planning any fix:
terraform plan -refresh-only      # "Objects have changed outside of Terraform": what, exactly
terraform apply -refresh-only     # accept reality into the state; changes no real object
Three honest answers to drift, and the question to ask before each:
1. **Put it back** (`apply`): the change was a mistake. *Does anyone depend on it now?*
2. **Put it in the code**: the change was right (a hotfix). Write it into the `.tf` files and apply, so the code is the
3. **Let another owner have that attribute**: something else legitimately changes it (an autoscaler's desired count,
tags added by a compliance tool): `lifecycle { ignore_changes = [desired_count] }` (module 3).
`-refresh=false` skips the refresh (fast on huge states) and is blind to drift: an emergency tool only.

steps.prompt: At 3 a.m. the on-call raised a load balancer's idle timeout in the console to stop an outage. Nobody touched the code. What does the next normal `terraform apply` of that folder do?
options: Sets the timeout back to the value in the code, and the outage may return
Keeps the new timeout, because it is newer
Writes the new timeout into the `.tf` file
steps.explain: The code is the desired state, so Terraform "corrects" the hotfix. That is why every manual fix must be followed, the same day, by a pull request that puts it into the code.

steps.title: A real plan with drift
body: This plan comes from the next step's machine: someone hot-fixed `nginx.conf` on the server and deleted `robots.txt`.
The local provider cannot tell a changed file from a deleted one (it compares content checksums), so both look
*deleted* and the plan wants to **create** them again, from the code: the hotfix would be overwritten. With AWS the
drift would show as `~` changes to individual attributes instead.

options: Only the state: it records the real objects' current values (or that they are gone); no real object is created, changed or deleted
The real objects, back to what the code says
The code: it writes the hotfix into the `.tf` files
Nothing at all; it is the same as `plan -refresh-only`
steps.explain: It is the reviewed replacement for the old `terraform refresh` command (which wrote the state without showing you anything first). After it, the code and the state may still disagree: the next normal plan shows exactly that difference.

steps.title: Keep the hotfix
prompt: Last night uploads failed (INC-2231). The on-call engineer fixed it by hand on the server: `out/nginx.conf` got a
`client_max_body_size 20m;` line. Someone also deleted `out/robots.txt` by mistake.
1. `terraform plan -refresh-only` in `~/infra/shop`: what changed outside Terraform?
2. Look at a normal `terraform plan`: what would it do to the hotfix?
3. Keep the hotfix **in the code** (the same line, inside the `server { }` block, right after `listen 443 ssl;`), bring
`robots.txt` back, and leave a plan with no changes.

checks.name: the hotfix is in the code
checks.fail: `main.tf` should contain `client_max_body_size 20m;` in the nginx config's content.

checks.name: the server has it
checks.cmd: cd ~/infra/shop && grep -q 'client_max_body_size 20m;' out/nginx.conf && grep -q 'listen 443 ssl;' out/nginx.conf
checks.fail: `out/nginx.conf` must still contain `client_max_body_size 20m;` (and the rest of the server block).

checks.name: robots.txt is back
checks.fail: `out/robots.txt` should exist again. Terraform can recreate it.

hints: `terraform plan -refresh-only` says both files *have been deleted* (their content no longer matches). A normal plan would write `nginx.conf` again **without** the hotfix.
In `main.tf`, add a line `  client_max_body_size 20m;` after `  listen 443 ssl;` inside the heredoc (`nano main.tf`).
`sed -i 's/^      listen 443 ssl;$/&\n      client_max_body_size 20m;/' main.tf`, then `terraform plan -out=tfplan` and `terraform apply tfplan`.
steps.explain: A plain `apply` would have "fixed" the drift by reverting the hotfix and broken uploads again. The rule on every team that runs Terraform: a manual change in production is followed by a pull request that puts it into the code, the same day. Many teams run `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` nightly and alert on exit 2, or use HCP Terraform's drift detection, so drift is found before the next deploy finds it.

items: Someone opened port 22 to 0.0.0.0/0 "for a minute"
The on-call raised a database's max connections to stop an outage
An ECS service's desired count is set by its autoscaler
A test bucket was made public by mistake
A compliance tool adds a `scanned-at` tag to every instance
A DNS TTL was lowered by hand for tonight's migration, which is now permanent
steps.explain: Security regressions go back at once. Legitimate fixes go into code so they survive the next apply. Attributes another system owns are ignored, narrowly: name the attribute, never `ignore_changes = all`, which hides every future drift on that resource.
